summary: Discusses design considerations for making Internet protocols extensible, aimed at people designing base protocols and their extensions. It uses case studies to show what works and what causes trouble. A companion document, RFC 4775, covers the procedures for extending protocols. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When you build a toy set, you should leave spots where new pieces can snap on later. This memo gives advice on leaving those spots so the toy does not break when someone adds more.

questions: how do protocol extensions cause interoperability failures
what is the difference between routine and major extensions
subtitle: Architectural principles for designing protocols that can safely evolve through extensions.

tldr.problem: Protocol extensions carry risks of interoperability failures, security vulnerabilities, and operational problems, yet extensions are necessary for protocols to adapt over time.
tldr.mechanism: Seven core architectural principles guide extensibility: limit it to what is reasonably anticipated, design for global interoperability, maintain architectural compatibility, avoid incompatible variations, ensure testability, coordinate parameters through registries, and take special care with critical infrastructure protocols.
tldr.outcome: Protocols designed with clear extensibility principles from the start are less likely to spawn incompatible variants and maintain interoperability as they evolve.

today: RFC 6709 is an Internet Standard-track Informational RFC from the Internet Architecture Board. It remains a reference for protocol design and is not superseded. It is intended as a companion to RFC 4775, which covers the formal procedures for extending IETF protocols.

sections.title: Why Protocol Extensibility Matters
sections.content:
Well-designed protocols incorporate mechanisms for future extension. As noted in RFC 5218 ("What Makes for a Successful Protocol"), successful protocols are often used in ways not originally anticipated. Protocols that can be extended safely and transparently allow incremental improvements and new features without requiring all implementations to change at once.

However, experience has shown that extensions carry significant risk. Poorly designed extensions cause interoperability failures, security vulnerabilities, and operational problems. The challenge is to design base protocols and their extensibility mechanisms carefully enough that future developers can add features without breaking existing deployments or creating incompatible variants.
sections.eli5: Good protocols can grow and change. Bad extensions make things break. This RFC teaches how to build protocols that grow safely.

sections.title: Routine and Major Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes between routine extensions and major extensions based on their risk. A routine extension does not require changes to the base protocol or existing implementations, and existing implementations can safely ignore it. Examples include new DHCP vendor options or RADIUS vendor-specific attributes.

A major extension risks breaking interoperability or introducing security problems. Major extensions modify the underlying protocol, change architectural assumptions, introduce new usage scenarios, alter the extension model itself, change protocol syntax, affect multiple protocols together, modify the security model, or impact performance. When identifying whether an extension is routine or major, the protocol document should provide clear guidance, so future developers understand what kind of review their work needs.
sections.eli5: Some add-ons are safe and small (routine). Others might break things (major). You should label which is which ahead of time.

sections.title: Architectural Principles for Extensibility
sections.content:
Seven core principles guide sound extensibility design. First, limit extensibility: do not make protocols more extensible than necessary, in order to optimize for the most common use cases. Second, design for global interoperability: extensions must interoperate with each other and with unextended implementations, even if they encounter each other unexpectedly on the global Internet.

Third, maintain architectural compatibility: extensions should fit the extension mechanisms envisioned in the base protocol, and protocol documents should identify what mechanisms exist and how to use them safely. Fourth, avoid incompatible variations: extension mechanisms should not be used to create protocol forks that fail to interoperate. Fifth, ensure testability: if the base protocol does not provide test cases for extension mechanisms, implementations may not be properly tested, and non-compliant behavior may go undetected until widely deployed.

Sixth, coordinate protocol parameters: parameter assignments must be registered through IANA to prevent conflicts. Seventh, protect critical protocols: extensions to Internet-critical protocols like DNS, BGP, or HTTP need special care and may require isolation mechanisms such as separate ports or processes.
sections.eli5: Extensibility should be simple, global, compatible, testable, coordinated and safe for critical systems. Do not make it too open or it breaks.

sections.title: Designing the Base Protocol for Extension
sections.content:
The RFC advises protocol designers to build extensibility into base protocols deliberately. Provide clear documentation of what an implementer must support and what the impact of each operation will be. Include guidance on how implementations should determine peer capabilities and negotiate use of extensions. Explain how implementations should handle extensions they do not understand.

Address backward compatibility explicitly: can an extended implementation negotiate with an unextended peer to find a common subset of functions? Document the underlying architectural assumptions and any operational considerations discovered after publication. Explain when it is appropriate to isolate new uses of a critical protocol from existing uses. Finally, provide clear guidance on when a data model extension is routine versus major, so that future extension designers understand the scope of review required.
sections.eli5: Tell people upfront: what is required, what happens with extensions, how to handle things we invent later, and when something is a big change.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability Risks
sections.content:
Extensions introduce several categories of risk. Version negotiation mistakes can cause incompatibilities: if a protocol does not clearly specify what happens when a new version number appears, implementations may fail or behave unexpectedly. The RFC surveys five versioning approaches used in practice, from no versioning support, to highest mutually supported version (HMSV), to major/minor versioning, to min/max versioning, each with different trade-offs.

Reserved field handling is critical: implementers must not reject packets with non-zero values in reserved fields, or the protocol will fail when those fields later acquire meaning. Parameter space exhaustion threatens protocols with small code point spaces: designers should either make the space large enough, provide vendor-specific extensions, or establish explicit reassignment procedures. The RFC reviews case studies where these mistakes caused problems, such as the EAP Type space exhaustion and BGP attribute tunneling instabilities.
sections.eli5: Versioning, reserved fields, and code points can break if not handled right. We learned these lessons the hard way.
